distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a license with an easement in gross and treats the neighbor's oral permission as a right the neighbor cannot take back.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses one permitted crossing with a prescriptive easement, which depends on long adverse use rather than permission from the owner.

prompt: To widen a public road, a city acquires a strip of an owner's front yard and pays the owner for that strip. The owner keeps the rest of the lot and asks whether this is simply a zoning change that lowered value but left possession unchanged. Which power did the city use?

options.text: A zoning change, treated as a taking because the strip lost value
Adverse possession, completed when the widened road opens to traffic
An area variance the owner must file in order to give up the strip
Eminent domain, taking the strip for just compensation

explanation: The city is taking a strip of private land for a public road and paying the owner. That is eminent domain, and the payment is just compensation. A zoning change that only lowers value, without this acquisition, is not the event on these facts.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the city's acquisition of the strip with a zoning change. A drop in value from zoning is not, by itself, this taking of the front yard.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a paid government taking with adverse possession, which is a claim based on long hostile occupancy rather than a road widening.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses eminent domain with an area variance. A variance is relief an owner seeks from a zoning board, not the city's acquisition of the strip.

prompt: At a closing in Nassau County, the seller delivers a deed that conveys the house "together with all right, title, and interest." The deed contains no covenants, and the seller will not promise that the title is good. Which deed is the seller giving?

options.text: A full covenant and warranty deed that promises the title is good
A quitclaim deed for whatever interest the grantor has
A bargain and sale deed with a covenant against the grantor's own acts
A referee's deed given after a court-ordered sale of the house

explanation: A quitclaim deed conveys whatever right, title, and interest the grantor has and includes none of the title warranties in a full covenant and warranty deed. Granting language limited to all right, title, and interest, with no promise that title is good, is quitclaim language.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a quitclaim with a full covenant and warranty deed, which carries covenants that the title is good against defects.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a quitclaim with a bargain and sale deed that still includes a covenant against the grantor's own acts.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the lack of a title promise with a referee's deed, which is used for a court-ordered sale rather than this seller's refusal to warrant title.
